title_content.content: Catalytic Asymmetric 1,4-Hydrocarbonation of 1,3-Enynes via Photoredox/Cobalt/Chromium Triple Catalysis

paragraph_content.content: Ju-Song Yang, Xing-Yu Wang, Yong-Yao Li, Fu-Min Zhang,* Xiao-Ming Zhang, and Yong-Qiang Tu*

Abstract: A synergistic photoredox/cobalt/chromium triple catalysis system for regioselective, enantioselective, and diastereoselective 1,4-hydrocarbonation of readily available 1,3-enyne precursors was explored, providing a modular synthetic platform for various trisubstituted axially chiral allenes bearing an extra central chirality. The protocol features a broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, excellent selectivity, and mild reaction conditions. Furthermore, a possible reaction mechanism is proposed based on numerous control experiments and density functional theory calculations.

Prochiral 1,3-enynes have received extensive attention in various asymmetric synthetic transformations using 1,4- difunctionalization procedures because of their multiple reaction sites and easily availability.<sup>[1–3]</sup> In particular, the catalytic asymmetric 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3- enynes has emerged as a method for accurately adding a hydrogen atom and carbon or heteroatom moiety in stationary conjugate π systems.<sup>[4–9,11]</sup> Accordingly, various transition metal (TM) catalysts (palladium,<sup>[4]</sup> rhodium,<sup>[5]</sup> copper,<sup>[6]</sup> scandium,<sup>[7]</sup> etc.) and organocatalysts<sup>[9]</sup> have been developed to synthesize silyl-, boryl-, and aryl-substituted axially chiral allenes via an ionic pathway (Scheme 1A, top). However, in sharp contrast to these ionic pathways, the radical 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes has yet to be exploited owing to the canonical migratory insertion of metal hydride into olefin units typically generating more stable alkyl metal intermediates rather than dissociative propargyl or short-lived allenic radicals.<sup>[10]</sup> To the best of our knowledge, only one example has been reported; very recently, Fu et al. achieved chiral nickel hydride–catalyzed asymmetric coupling of prochiral 1,3-enynes with racemic secondary alkyl electrophiles to simultaneously produce central and axial chirality (Scheme 1B, bottom).<sup>[11]</sup> Therefore, exploring new radical formation modes from 1,3- enynes to achieve mechanistic innovations and obtain useful multiple chiral allene architectures is urgent.

As the radical equivalent of Brønsted acid proton transfer, TM-catalyzed (cobalt (Co), iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), etc.) metal hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions of alkenes represent a powerful and practical method for constructing diverse C�C and C-heteroatom bonds.<sup>[12–18]</sup> Among them, tandem MHAT/1,2-addition was developed by Shenvi et al. (2018)<sup>[14]</sup> and Shi et al. (2021)<sup>[15]</sup> to couple alkyl-substituted olefins, allenes, or 1,3-dienes with radicalophilic imines or aldehydes, respectively. For the catalytic asymmetric version, a recent breakthrough was elegantly disclosed by Wang et al., employing modified photoredox/Co/chromium (Cr) triple–catalytic systems for enantioselective 1,2-addition of benzoyloxy-substituted 1,3- dienes to synthesize aldehydes bearing an indispensable benzoyloxy protecting group, in which the oxygen atom in the substrates plays an essential coordination role (Scheme 1B).<sup>[16]</sup> Retrospectively, MHAT-meditated regioand chemoselective 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of more structurally complex 1,3-enyens substrates was rarely studied except for a remarkable racemic version of research work by Carreira’s group in 2006;<sup>[17]</sup> unfortunately, only azodicarboxylate was used as an electrophile, which led to the corresponding propargyl derivatives. To fill this gap, particularly the catalytic asymmetric version, we speculated that if other electrophiles, such as aldehydes or imines, were reacted with the chiral propargyl radical species derived from prochiral 1,3-enynes, the unconventional asymmetric 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes would occur; furthermore, the novel synthetic method would provide an efficient approach toward α-allenol, a unique structural motif bearing both central and axial chirality, widely found in natural products, pharmaceuticals, functional materials, chiral ligands, and key synthetic intermediates (Figure 1).<sup>[19–20]</sup> However, this attractive strategy has several synthetic challenges that must be addressed. 1) Unlike the 1,2-addition of an allyl group via a suitable six-membered transition state, the 1,2-addition of propargyl-containing intermediates to aldehydes via an extremely distorted cyclic transition state leads to unmanageable regioselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity.<sup>[21a–c,24d]</sup> 2) Although the reaction sequences involving TM hydride species, 1,3-enynes, and electrophiles can be successively and efficiently controlled according to the designed reaction process, some undesirable side reactions (i.e., propargylation and/or allenylation of the reaction intermediates and electrophile reduction) should be suppressed as much as possible.<sup>[21a–b,27a]</sup> 3) Simultaneous control of axial and central chirality is difficult in the reaction procedure involving the TM–proparyl species.<sup>[11,21d]</sup> 4) Most importantly, two or more catalytic cycles should be processed synergistically in multicatalysis systems; otherwise, the incompatibility of multiple catalysts and reaction partners can lead to undesirable mono-catalysis cycle processes, which are common in complex reaction procedures.<sup>[21e–f,23,25a]</sup> Although the aforementioned problems likely exist in this challenging asymmetric transformation, we intended to address them using our recently developed spirocyclic–pyrrolidine (SPD)–oxazoline ligands<sup>[22]</sup> combined with other TMs as an efficient catalytic system.

Notably, the more attractive redox-neutral three-component reaction of terminal 1,3-enynes via a radical addition mode, was successively established by Glorius and Wang et al., affording the racemic propargylated and chiral allenylated products, respectively (Scheme

Inspired by these and MHAT chemistry, to develop a viable and alternative manner to form essential propargyl radical, herein, we report a protocol for radical-involved reductive coupling of Z/E-mixed internal and terminal 1,3-enynes with aldehydes via a tandem MHAT/1,2-addition transformation sequence facilitated by a photoredox/Co/Cr triple–catalytic system (Scheme 1D). This protocol successfully afforded operational connection between readily accessible 1,3-enyne feedstocks and multiple-substituted axially chiral allenes bearing a C-stereogenic center, an important structural motif (Figure 1). Furthermore, mechanistic studies and density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed the origin of the regioselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity.

Based on our design, we commenced catalytic asymmetric radical–involved reductive coupling studies using triisopropyl(pent-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)silane (1 a) and benzaldehyde (2 a) as the model substrates. Initially, optimization studies were performed using cobalt tetraphenylporphine (CoTPP, 1 mol %), chromium(II) chloride (CrCl<sub>2</sub>, 13 mol %), and photosensitizer Ir-I (1 mol %) as the triplecatalytic metal species, our developed SPD (L1) as a chiral ligand, Hantzsch ester (HE) as the electron and proton donor, and tetrahydrofuran (THF) (0.05 M) as the solvent. The reactions were performed under 70 W blue light emitting diode irradiation for 16 h. As expected, using L1 as the chiral ligand resulted in the desired α-allenol 3a in high yield and good stereoselectivity (Table 1, entry 1), whereas other nitrogen-containing ligands (L2–L9) were less effective (Table 1, entries 2–9). Subsequently, the reaction solvents, MHAT catalyst, and other reaction parameters were varied, respectively. Using dimethoxyethane as the solvent caused a slight increase in yield (87 %) and stereoselectivity (96% ee, and >20 :1 dr) (Table 1, entry 10), whereas chlorinated solvents such as 1,2-dichloroethane and chlorobenzene were unsuitable for this transformation (Table 1, entries 11 and 12, respectively). Notably, minor inseparable propargylation regioisomers were detected when polar dimethylformamide was used as the solvent (Table 1, entry 13). Furthermore, the reaction hardly proceeded using iron(tetraporphyrinato) chloride (FeTPPCl) or tetraphenylporphyrinato Mn(III) chloride (MnTPPCl) as the MHAT catalyst instead of CoTPP (Table 1, entries 14 and 15, respectively). The control experiments demonstrated that all of the reagents and conditions in the synergistic triple catalysis were required because no reaction occurred when the light source, the photosensitizer, CoTPP, or CrCl was separately removed (Table 1, entry 16). Therefore, the reaction parameters listed in entry 10 (Table 1) were selected as the optimal reaction conditions for further investigations.

Notably, unlike the previous radical 1,4- difunctionalization studies,<sup>[27a]</sup> the transformation was compatible with terminal and cyclic or acyclic trisubstituted alkene units of 1,3-enynes, albeit with a slight decrease in the reaction outcomes with increasing steric hindrance (3 d vs. 3 f vs. 3 g). Next, the substrate scope of aromatic aldehydes was investigated (Table 2). Mono-substituted benzaldehydes bearing different electronic properties and substitution patterns produced the expected products 4a– 4e, 4i–4j, and 4 n in moderate to high yields (61 %–90%) and excellent enantioselectivities (91%–97 % ees). Substituents at the 2,6-, 3,5-, or 3,4-positions of the phenyl ring had almost no influence on the enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity (4 k, 95 % ee, 13: 1 dr; 4l, 96 % ee, 17 :1 dr; 4m, 94 % ee, >20 :1 dr; and 4o, 87 % ee, >20 :1 dr). These results were superior to previous reports,<sup>[27a]</sup> particularly the diastereoselectivity. Notably, aldehydes derived from medicinally important condensed and heterocyclic arenes, including thiazole, oxazole, pyridine, benzothiophene, and indole, were successfully transformed (4 p–4 x). Furthermore, the generality of aliphatic aldehydes was investigated. Aliphatic aldehydes with diverse linear or steric alkyl chains participated efficiently in the 1,4-hydrocarbonation of 1,3-enynes (5 a, 5g–5 h). Finally, aliphatic aldehydes with different functional groups at the distinct terminal position, including phenyl, benzyl ether, phthalimido, chlorine atom, and trifluoromethyl, were compatible with the optimal reaction conditions (5 b–5 f, respectively). To further confirm the robustness of this triple catalysis system, late-stage diversification of structurally complex molecules and commercially available chiral aldehydes was performed (Figure 2A). Highly functionalized α-allenols 6a– 6 c possessing continuous multiple stereogenic centers were obtained as single diastereomers, predominantly determined using enantioselective recognition of chiral SPD-series ligands. Notably, the absolute configuration of product 6b was determined using X-ray single-crystal diffraction. Moreover, aldehydes derived from the anti-inflammatory drug ibuprofen and the anti-inflammatory and antigout drug probenecid were efficiently synthesized under optimal reaction conditions, leading to products 6 d–6 f.

paragraph_content.content: Furthermore, aldehydes derived from natural products, including (� )-β-citronellol and estrone, showed excellent diastereoselectivities. Inspired by recent reports on hydrogen atom transfer (HAT)-initiated alkene isomerization,<sup>[13d,28]</sup> a tandem isomerization sequence using MHAT and 1,2-addition transformation was conducted using nonconjugated 1,4-enyne substance 6i under the slightly modified reaction conditions. The corresponding 1,5-hydrocarbonation product 5 b was obtained, which was further transformed into the multisubstituted THF derivative 6j in an axial-to-central chirality transfer manner. More importantly, the key intermediate 6m was obtained using our protocol for the formal synthesis of the natural product pheromone.<sup>[20f]</sup>

A series of control experiments were designed and conducted to understand the triple catalysis system. First, in the presence of radical scavengers (2.0 equiv. of allyl sulfone, (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxyl (TEMPO), or 2,6-ditert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT)), the reactions were almost entirely inhibited (Figure 3A). The 1,3-enynes 6o containing a three-membered ring, was subjected to the optimal reaction condition, affording a ring-opening product 6 p in ~63 % yield. The possible formation pathway was as follows: the 6o initially occurred MHAT process to generate the intermediate Int I, which fast collapsed toward intermediate Int II. The radical Int II subsequently went through intramolecular 5-exo-dig cyclization to provide vinyl radical Int III, which finally yielded the isolated product 6 p via H-atom abstraction (Figure 3B). Moreover, cyclopropanecarbaldehyde smoothly produced the corresponding product 5i without the isolation of radical ring-opening coupling product, except for the possibility of ketyl radical intermediates in the triple catalytic system. Subsequently, the results of the interval light–dark reaction experiments and the estimated quantum yield of Φ =0.25, both indicated that the current transformation occurred via a photoredox process rather than a radical-chain pathway (Figure 3C). Therefore, the propargyl radical species were unequivocally involved in the current transformation. A linear correlation between the enantioselectivities of α-allenol and the enantiopurities of chiral ligand L1 was observed, suggesting that this reductive 1,2-addition was promoted by the ligated catalyst in a monomeric state (Figure 3D).<sup>[29a]</sup> The Stern–Volmer luminescence quenching studying demonstrated that the excited state of Ir-photocatalyst were quenched by all CoPc, CrCl / L1 and HE, rather than the 1,3-enyne or aldehydes. Among these, the Hantzsch ester is a more effective quencher at the similar concentration level, according with a possible reductive quenching pathway (Figure 3E).<sup>[30]</sup> The parallel and competition kinetic isotope effect (KIE) experiments were also conducted to clarify the influence of deuteration at aldehyde group (Figure 3F). And the parallel and competition KIE value were determined to be 0.91 and 0.88, respectively, showing a substantial inverse secondary isotopic effect. Finally, when HE was replaced by its deuterated analogue under the optimal reaction conditions, the corresponding products 3a– D were isolated with ~60 % deuterium only at the distal C4 position, suggesting that the MHAT process is irreversible in this catalytic system (Figure 3G). Additionally, DFT calculations were performed to reveal the MHAT process.<sup>[30]</sup> The results were as follows. 1) The energy of the transition state in which MHAT occurred at the C4 position was 6.5 kcal/mol lower than that at the C3 position, and the free energy barrier of the reverse process was 23.4 kcal/mol, suggesting that the MHAT process was regiospecific and irreversible. 2) The energy barrier of homolysis for the propargyl or allenyl Co species was substantially negative, indicating that they were too unstable to easily homolyze to generate the related radicals.

Finally, the target allenes are obtained, with free Cr(III) released by hydrolysis and reduced to Cr(II) via Ir(II) for the next catalytic cycle, thus completing the third catalytic cycle.

DFT calculations were also conducted to understand the detailed Cr-mediated 1,2-addition mechanism and the role of the SPD–oxazoline ligand on regioselectivity and stereoselectivity (Figure 4B). According to previous literature<sup>[21a–b]</sup> and our proposed reaction mechanism, the monomeric Cr complex <sup>5</sup>IN1 was identified as a reactive catalyst and set as the relative zero point for the Gibbs free energy. Initially, radical recombination occurred on different faces of the propargyl radical to generate two stereogenic propargyl Cr(III) complexes, <sup>4</sup>IN2–S and <sup>4</sup>IN2–R. After the Cr(III) species coordinated with the aldehyde, the enantioselective 1,2-addition led to the O-bounded Cr species <sup>4</sup>IN4–R R, with the transition state <sup>4</sup>TS1–R R (9.9 kcal/mol). These results were also demonstrated by the twist angles of the alkynyl silicon units and the surface distance projection map of the molecules (see Figure S7 for details).<sup>[32b,d]</sup> Overall, the steric hindrance feature of the Cr–SPD–oxazoline catalyst produces a stereoscopic pattern of 1,2-addition via a distinct distorted cyclic transition state.

We developed a photoinduced Co/Cr dual-catalyzed 1,4- hydrocarbonation reaction to couple prochiral 1,3-enynes with radicalophilic aldehydes under mild, eco-friendly reaction conditions, producing a series of axially chiral allenes bearing a centrally chiral secondary alcohol unit in high yields with excellent regioselectivity, enantioselectivity, and diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic investigations and DFT calculations were conducted to elucidate the origin of the regioselectivity and stereoselectivity of this asymmetric transformation.
